headline: Gake shifted from the older pronunciation kake and was first attested in 1280.

sources.quote: Shift from older pronunciation kake. First attested in 1280.

May be a shift in usage from compounding element kake as in the synonymous terms 懸路 (kakeji), 懸道 (kakemichi, “cliff road, steep mountain road”), where the kake comes from verb 懸ける (kakeru, “to set into; to set across”), from the way the road would be set into the cliff or mountain.

The change from kake to gake apparently happened some time during the Edo period (1603–1868). This term is recorded as Caqe (then-current Portuguese orthography for modern romanization kake) in the 1603 Nippo Jisho Japanese-Portuguese dictionary.

headline: Muyō is 無 (mu-, “non-”) plus 用 (yō, “use”).

sources.quote: 無(む) (mu-, “non-”) + 用(よう) (yō, “use”).

headline: Hinjaku is probably from the Middle Chinese compound 貧弱, literally “poor + weak”, or may have been coined in Japan from 貧 (hin, “poor”) plus 弱 (jaku, “weak”).

sources.quote: Probably from Middle Chinese compound 貧弱 (MC bin nyak, literally “poor + weak”). Compare modern Mandarin 貧弱／贫弱 (pínruò, “poor and weak”).
Alternatively, may have been coined in Japan of Middle Chinese-derived elements 貧 (hin, “poor”) + 弱 (jaku, “weak”).

headline: Kozue was originally 木 (ko-, the bound form of 木 (ki, “tree”)) plus 末 (sue, “tip, end”), with sue voiced to zue by rendaku.

sources.quote: Originally a compound of 木(こ) (ko-, the 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 木(き) (ki, “tree”)) + 末(すえ) (sue, “tip, end”).
The sue changes to zue as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Hannō was coined by Iwakawa Tomotarō in 1884 as a translation of English reaction, and the ō of 応 became nō by renjō.

sources.quote: Coined by Japanese educator and zoologist Iwakawa Tomotarō in 1884 in his work 生物学語彙 (Seibutsugaku goi, “A biological vocabulary in English, Latin and Japanese”) as a translation of English reaction.
The ō reading for 応 changes to nō as an instance of renjō (連(れん)声(じょう)).

headline: Tsukekuwaeru is 付け (tsuke, the stem of 付ける (tsukeru, “to attach”)) plus 加える (kuwaeru, “to add”).

headline: Mine is 御 (mi, honorific prefix) plus 峰 (ne, “peak”), in reference to the 神 (kami, “god or spirit”) at the top of a mountain.

sources.quote: From 御(み) (mi, honorific prefix) + 峰(ね) (ne, “peak”), in reference to the 神 (kami, “god or spirit”) at the top of a mountain. Now the standard spelling for a peak.
Compare 道 (michi, “road”).
